links.title: How is failed replication handled?
links.body: Buckit queues failed replication operations and retries those operations until replication succeeds.

links.title: What are Replication Workers?
links.body: Buckit uses a replication queuing system with multiple concurrent replication workers operating on that queue.

links.body: Check under Monitoring/Drives on the left hand  menu to see Drive and Bucket Healing status

links.title: How is Erasure Coding used to Protect Data?
links.body: Buckit erasure coding is a data redundancy and  availability feature that allows Buckit deployments to  automatically reconstruct objects on-the-fly despite  the loss of multiple drives or nodes in the cluster.

links.title: Recover After Hardware failure
links.body: Depending on the deployment topology and  selected erasure code parity, Buckit can tolerate loss  of up to half the drives or nodes in the deployment  while maintaining read access to objects.

links.title: Site Failure Recovery
links.body: Buckit can make the loss of an entire site, while  significant, a relatively minor incident. Site recovery depends on the replication option you use for the site.

links.title: Node Failure Recovery
links.body: If a Buckit node suffers complete hardware failure, the node begins healing operations once it rejoins the  deployment.

links.title: What is Buckit Healing?
links.body: Healing is Buckit’s ability to restore data after some event causes data loss. Data loss can come from bit rot, drive loss, or node loss.

links.title: Understand Buckit Healing Using mc
links.body: The mc admin heal command scans for objects that are damaged or corrupted and heals those objects.

links.title: What is Bit Rot?
links.body: Bit rot is data corruption that occurs without the user’s knowledge. Buckit combats bit rot with hashing and erasure coding.

links.title: Overview of Buckit Erasure Coding
links.body: Through this Buckit video you will learn about Buckit erasure coding, including erasure sets, erasure parity, and stripe size. You will also learn about how the Reed-Solomon algorithm can be optimized for storage efficiency (yielding cost savings) or data lost protection (number of servers and drives that can fail). The video also walks through the Buckit Erasure Code calculator, considerations for cluster design and the command line syntax needed to establish an erasure code deployment.

links.title: What is the Scanner?
links.body: One of several low-priority processes Buckit runs to check lifecycle management rules, bucket or site replication status, as well as object bit rot and healing

links.title: Lifecycle Management Object Scanner Considerations
links.body: Buckit uses a scanner process to check objects against all configured lifecycle management rules. High IO workloads or limited system resources may delay application of lifecycle management rules
